title: Composition

learn.summary: Composition is deciding what goes in the frame, what stays out, and where everything sits — the one skill that transfers across every camera ever made. The masters' consensus: simplify. Most weak photos fail from clutter, not gear; every element in the frame should earn its place.

do: Before each photo today, name your subject in one word, then remove one distracting thing from the frame by moving your feet.

children.title: Rule of Thirds & Breaking It

learn.summary: Divide the frame with two horizontal and two vertical lines; placing subjects on the lines or their four intersections usually beats dead center. Horizons go on the top or bottom third, never the middle — unless you are breaking the rule on purpose, as centered symmetry (think formal portraits or reflections) does powerfully. Learn it, use it, then outgrow it.

do: Turn on your phone camera's grid overlay today, shoot ten photos placing subjects on intersections, then shoot two deliberately dead-centered symmetric ones.

children.title: Leading Lines

learn.summary: Roads, railings, rivers, and shadows act as arrows steering the viewer's eye through the frame — ideally toward the subject, disastrously toward an exit. Diagonals feel dynamic; converging lines add depth like a vanishing point in a drawing. Once you start seeing lines, sidewalks become compositions.

do: On one walk this week, make five photographs where a line (path, fence, shadow) visibly leads to your subject.

children.title: Framing & Layers

learn.summary: Shooting through something — a doorway, branches, a window's reflection — puts a frame within the frame and instantly adds depth. Strong images often stack three layers: foreground, subject, background, each doing a job. This is how a flat rectangle fakes three dimensions.

do: Shoot three photos today through something: a doorway, foliage, a gap between people — the frame must touch at least two edges of your image.

children.title: Negative Space

learn.summary: Empty space is not wasted space — a small subject against a vast plain sky or wall gains drama, scale, and breathing room. Negative space is also where minimalism lives: one subject, one background, nothing else. When a photo feels cluttered, the fix is usually more emptiness, not more subject.

do: Make three photographs this week where the subject occupies less than 20 percent of the frame and the rest is deliberately empty.

children.title: Change Your Perspective

learn.summary: Eye-level from standing height is the world's default view — and therefore the most boring. Crouch to a child's or pet's eye line, shoot straight up, climb stairs and shoot down, or put the camera centimeters from the ground. Moving your feet is the cheapest lens you will ever own.

do: Photograph one ordinary object from five heights and angles today — knees, ground level, above, behind — and pick the least expected winner.
